n: In this lecture we introduce bioethics and consider why this discipline is needed. Bioethics is a field aimed at understanding, discussing and resolving the moral problems that arise from advances in biomedicine and from the practice of healthcare. It is an area of interdisciplinary research, open debate and political decision-making. In 1994 the World Health Organization recommended introducing a bioethics course in all medical schools. The key idea: ethics is the science that studies morality, and bioethics is one branch of applied ethics.

t: Changes in medicine and new problems
n: What is changing in medicine? The fundamental sciences are developing rapidly, yet the consequences of many new technologies are uncertain or dangerous. Clinical medicine is widening its capacity to influence the human body, offspring, the psyche and the process of dying. The chain of problems is as follows: the fundamental sciences advance, new technologies appear, their consequences prove uncertain or dangerous, and moral and legal questions arise. The Hippocratic Oath is not abolished, but its basic provisions change radically.

t: Bioethics is the ethics of patients
n: Bioethics is the ethics of patients. The principles of bioethics are not direct instructions to the physician; they are foundations from which specific decisions can later be reached. These principles define the rights and duties of patients more than those of physicians. That is why bioethics is called the ethics of patients: these are rules that take into account and protect the interests of every person in the position of a patient. There are also disputed questions: when does life begin and when does it end? Is there a limit to sustaining the life of a gravely ill, dying patient?

t: Definitions of bioethics: narrow and broad sense
n: Definitions of bioethics. In the narrow sense, bioethics denotes the whole range of ethical problems in the relationship between physician and patient. In the broad sense, it studies the social, ecological and medical problems concerning humans and all living organisms. Attention: the narrow sense is not identical to the broad sense; the narrow sense covers only the physician–patient relationship. In 1927 F. Jahr demanded respect for animals and plants as well. The Oxford dictionary defines bioethics as the ethical problems of medicine and biology.

t: Case analysis 1: new technology and a moral question
n: Case analysis. The situation is this: medical technology can artificially sustain the life of a patient for whom death was previously inevitable. At the same time, new possibilities have appeared, such as artificial insemination, cloning and transplantology. The question from the source: is there a limit to sustaining the life of a gravely ill, dying patient? Another question: how are the interests of the patient and of society balanced in such a situation? In the UNESCO declaration, the interests of the individual are placed above the interests of science or society.

Test yourself with quick questions. First question: whose interests does bioethics protect? Answer: the interests of every person in the position of a patient, which is why it is called the ethics of patients. Second question: what did the WHO recommend in 1994? Answer: to introduce a bioethics course in all medical schools worldwide. Third question: what is the nature of the principles of bioethics? Answer: they are not direct instructions to the physician, but foundations from which specific decisions can be reached.

Ethics, morality and Aristotle. Morality is one of the primary mechanisms regulating human behaviour and relations between people. Morality is studied by a separate science, ethics. This science was founded by the Greek philosopher Aristotle. Ethics, from the Greek “ethos”, meaning character or custom, is the philosophical science that studies manners and morality. Attention: morality and ethics are not the same thing. Compassion, justice, friendship and solidarity are the moral foundation of human development.

t: Branches of ethics: theoretical and normative
n: Branches of ethics. Ethics is divided into two branches: theoretical and normative. Theoretical ethics studies the origin and regularities of morality. Normative ethics, in turn, establishes the criteria that guide behaviour. Applied ethics applies the ideas formed in normative ethics to specific situations of moral choice. Attention: theoretical ethics explains, whereas normative ethics shows the way.

How did applied ethics arise? Technological capabilities grew, interference with nature and global risks intensified, and new problems and new approaches to solving them became necessary. This is how the types of applied ethics appeared: political ethics, journalistic ethics, business ethics, ecoethics and bioethics. Casuistry, from the Latin “casus”, a case, means the examination of many situations and precedents; applied ethics is also viewed in this way. An example: once genetics emerged, a new question arose: is artificial reproduction advisable?

t: Case analysis 2: genetics and new questions
n: Case analysis: genetics and new questions. With the emergence of genetics, humanity faced questions that had never arisen before. First question: is artificial reproduction acceptable? Second question: should society attempt to create animals and humans by means of genetic engineering? A question for discussion: why was traditional ethics not prepared for this? The growth of technology brings new problems and a new scale, which demand new solutions.

Traditional trends in ethics. The trends are distinguished by their leading concept: happiness, goodness, duty, love, sympathy, justice. The ethics of happiness is also called felicitology. The ethics of goodness is called aretology; the word “arete” means virtue. The ethics of duty is deontology. Hedonism and cynicism are also counted as separate types of ethics.

The normativity of traditional ethics. Traditional ethics is normative: it sought to realise values and turn them into norms of behaviour. A value serves as an imperative, that is, a moral demand, an ideal and a norm. The worth of justice lies in its realisation. Attention: normativity is not the same as moralising or the promotion of morals; the two must not be confused. Normative programmes rely on experience and logic. In this respect philosophical ethics differs sharply from religious preaching.

Absolutism and relativism. Kant is a representative of absolutism: in his view, morality is a self-sufficient supreme value that is not derived from any other sphere. Kantian morality serves as the foundation for law, religion, art and politics. Relativism, by contrast, tries to derive morality from nature, society, culture, hereditary predisposition and the like. That is, in absolutism morality needs no foundation, whereas in relativism it is derived from other spheres.

Schopenhauer and irrationalism. At the beginning of the nineteenth century Schopenhauer criticised the classical conceptions and the main ideas of traditional ethics and founded the irrationalist trend. He rejected two ideas: that man is rational and capable of self-control, and that man strives for the well-being of others. In his view, the world is governed not by reason but by an unconscious “will”. The will is characterised as “evil”, “egoistic” and “depraved”. The approach is this: do not idealise man, do not try to change him, accept him as he is.

The second block of quick questions. Question 1: what is normative ethics? Answer: ethics directed at turning a value into a norm of behaviour, at seeking an ideal applicable in life. Question 2: which trend does Kant represent? Answer: absolutism, because he regarded morality as self-sufficient and as the foundation of other spheres. Question 3: which two ideas did Schopenhauer oppose? Answer: the idea of human rationality and the idea of human virtue. Attention: do not confuse normativity with moralising or religious propaganda.

Psychology and sociology of morality. Nietzsche and Freud developed Schopenhauer's conception in detail. They drew attention to the hidden, unconscious aspects of behaviour, which led to the psychology of morality. The departure from traditional conceptions found expression in the sociology of morality; its representative is Weber. Weber studied the role of the Protestant economic ethic.

Metaethics and descriptive ethics. Moore separated theoretical ethics from normative ethics: a moral judgement does not follow from facts. Metaethics carries out a logical analysis of the language of morality; it gave up the normative function, responsibility and the needs of practical life. Its founder is G. Moore, at the beginning of the twentieth century. Descriptive ethics, from the English “describe”, describes behaviour without laying down rules. It empirically describes the customs of different eras and cultures.

Case analysis: distinguishing the trends. A teaching example: two students assess the same action. One justifies it by the custom of a culture, the other rejects it by a universal demand. Let us recall: in absolutism, with Kant, morality is a self-sufficient value, not derived from any other sphere, and it serves as the foundation for law, religion, art and politics. Relativism tries to derive morality from nature, social reality, authoritative sources, hereditary predisposition and culture. Question: which trend does each student represent, and why?

t: Stages in the development of medical ethics and bioethics
n: Stages in the development of medical ethics and bioethics. In the 1970s transplantology and genetic engineering gave rise to new moral problems. After the crimes of the Nazi physicians were exposed, the Nuremberg Code was adopted in 1947. Potter introduced the term “bioethics” into scientific usage in 1969 and is regarded as its founder. Timeline: the fifth century BC, the Sophists; 1927, Jahr and the bioethical imperative; 1947, the Nuremberg Code; 1969 to 1971, Potter; 1978, the Encyclopedia of Bioethics.

t: The Sophists and Fritz Jahr's bioethical imperative
n: The Sophists and Fritz Jahr's bioethical imperative. In the fifth century BC the Sophists discovered that the laws of culture differ substantially from the laws of nature. It was emphasised that natural needs are the same everywhere, whereas customs, laws and manners are diverse and changeable. Hence the problem arose of comparing different laws and customs in order to determine the best. In 1927 the German pastor Fritz Jahr set out the bioethical imperative in opposition to Kant's categorical imperative: animals and plants also deserve respect.

The Nuremberg Code, 1947. The crimes of the Nazis were exposed: nearly half a million people were sterilised, and more than 100 thousand mentally ill people were forcibly subjected to euthanasia. In 1947 a set of 10 ethical rules for conducting medical experiments on humans was adopted, and it became the first international document on bioethics. The Code is based on the materials of the International Military Tribunal and was an appendix to the verdict passed on the Nazi physicians. The principles of the Code were not a requirement of law but norms of morality, and were not regarded as binding.

t: Van Rensselaer Potter and “Bridge to the Future”
n: Van Rensselaer Potter. The American oncologist Van Rensselaer Potter, 1911 to 2001, introduced the term “bioethics” into scientific usage; he is also known as a humanist scholar. The aim: to form a new science that would be a bridge between two cultures, science and the humanities. Potter's idea: to preserve life on Earth, the humanities and biology should unite, and the long-term consequences of progress should be taken into account.

Global bioethics. Potter called this system of norms global bioethics; it unites three trends. The aim is to develop ethical norms for the long-term survival of humankind as a species. Bioethics should become a bridge linking medical ethics and ecoethics on a worldwide scale. That is, on one side medical ethics, on the other environmental ethics, and bioethics unites them.

t: Reasons for the emergence of bioethics
n: Reasons for the emergence of bioethics. Bioethics is a new cultural phenomenon that arose in response to the threats of rapid scientific and technological progress, in order to protect basic moral values. Objective reasons: progress in biological and medical research, scientific and technological development, the computer and information boom. Subjective reasons: the growth of human rights and moral responsibility, and the globalisation of world processes. The result: the technological re-equipment of medicine, the transformation of traditional ethics, and a new understanding of the physician–patient relationship.

t: Bioethics committees and bioethics in Uzbekistan
n: Bioethics committees. Committees that deal permanently with these problems exist within UNESCO, the WHO, the World Medical Association and the Council of Europe. In many countries bioethics committees work at several levels: central, regional and local, that is, committees in a hospital or institute. A bioethics committee has also been established under the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Uzbekistan. And under the Ibn Sina International Foundation, the National Bioethics Committee of the Republic of Uzbekistan has been set up.

Tasks of bioethics committees. The committees ensure interaction among physicians, patients and relatives; in difficult cases a philosopher, a clergyman and a lawyer take part. The precedent for establishing committees belongs to the USA: the cause was protest against ethical violations in drug research. In Uzbekistan the first national ethics committee was established under the Ministry of Health in 2000; its head is Academician M.S. Abdullakhodjaeva. Today in the USA and Europe any clinical or medical research can be conducted only after approval by a committee. The five tasks of committees: discussion, oversight, consultation, education and policy.

Case analysis: lessons of Nuremberg. The crimes of the Nazis were exposed: nearly half a million people were sterilised, and more than 100 thousand incurably mentally ill people were forcibly subjected to euthanasia. Extremely dangerous medical experiments were carried out on concentration camp prisoners; medical practice sank to the level of “ethical zero”. In response, the Nuremberg Code, 10 ethical rules, was adopted in 1947; it became the first international document, but not a law, rather a norm of morality. Question: why was the Code adopted as a norm of morality, and how did this affect the responsibility of scientists?

The third block of quick questions. Question 1: who first used the term “bioethics” in 1927? Question 2: how many ethical rules for conducting medical experiments on humans does the Nuremberg Code, 1947, contain? Question 3: in which book did Potter first use the term “bioethics”, and when was it published? Attention: Jahr, 1927, and Potter are not the same person. Jahr was the first to use the term; Potter introduced it into scientific usage in 1969, and his book appeared in 1971.

The worldview of anthropocentrism. Here only the human being is valuable, and other beings have no independent value: “everything is for man”. Aristotle's school regarded animals as created for man; his follower Xenophon simplified this. This worldview is close to egocentrism, racism and nationalism; it taught people to look at nature as a “warehouse”. The chain of consequences: nature is regarded as man's warehouse, the environment is polluted, the threat of a global ecological catastrophe arises, and the need for biocentrism appears.

Meyer's typology. J.R. Meyer distinguishes types of worldview according to whom moral duty is directed. In sociocentrism, duty is directed to all members of the group. In pathocentrism, duty is directed to all sentient beings; in anthropocentrism, only to humans; and in biocentrism, to all living beings, that is, to “bios”. Attention: anthropocentrism is not the same as biocentrism. In biocentrism the circle of duty is not limited to humans.

Biocentrism and ahimsa. In biocentrism all living creatures have the right to live, and the focus is not only on the human being but on the whole of “bios”. The rights of “bios” should be protected by law. Ahimsa is the principle of non-violence and of not harming any living thing; it is the philosophical basis of biocentrism and the main rule of yama in yoga. Anthropocentrism, by contrast, says “everything is for man” and likens nature to man's warehouse. Applying biocentrism in practice requires a change in attitude to consumption: preserving animal habitats and putting an end to deforestation.

Albert Schweitzer's universal ethics. In the book “Culture and Ethics”, 1924, Schweitzer founded the “ethics of reverence for life”. A moral person does not pluck a flower needlessly and rescues an insect that has fallen into a puddle with a leaf or a twig. Remember: general, universal, unlimited. General means a single foundation of morality; universal means relating to all forms of life; unlimited means that the circle of responsibility is not restricted. “Ethics is unlimited responsibility toward all living beings.”

t: Compassion, altruism and the science of mercy
n: Compassion, altruism and the science of mercy. Altruism is a sense of responsibility for other people. Attention: altruism is not egoism; in egoism personal benefit comes first. Compassion is the supreme value acquired by humans in the course of evolution; it requires the cultivation of such qualities as mercy, benevolence and kindness. As this ability developed, humans learned to sympathise with all creatures capable of feeling pain and suffering. Bioethics is the most developed part of applied ethics, and it is also interpreted as a new science of mercy and a new worldview.

Case analysis: choice of worldview. The situation: to achieve a scientific goal, the interests of a human being or an animal are pushed aside, and they are regarded merely as objects of intervention. In anthropocentrism only human interests matter, and other beings have no independent value: “everything is for man”. In biocentrism, by contrast, the human being has a moral duty toward all living beings; the focus is on “bios”, that is, life. Question: which worldview does this situation correspond to, and why is it dangerous? History has confirmed the danger of sacrificing life and health “for science and society”.

t: The four historical models of medical ethics
n: The four historical models of medical ethics. Historically, four main models of medical ethics are distinguished; they place different demands on the physician–patient relationship. In the Hippocratic model the demand is “do no harm”, in the Paracelsian model “do good”, in the deontological model moral impeccability, and in the biomedical model respect for rights and dignity. Attention: the demand “do no harm” appears both in the Hippocratic model and among the main principles of the biomedical model. For centuries the Hippocratic Oath has been the standard of the physician's moral consciousness; the new medicine radically changes its basic provisions.

t: The structure of bioethics and its main problems
n: The structure of bioethics. UNESCO is the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. According to its charter, bioethics consists of four parts: theoretical and philosophical bioethics; biomedical ethics, that is, clinical bioethics; pharmaceutical bioethics; and the ethics of drug development and testing, that is, the ethics of clinical trials. The range of problems is wide, from patients' rights to euthanasia. Attention: biomedical ethics is a part of bioethics; the two are not the same concept.

The main problems of bioethics. The first group: protecting the rights of patients, that is, people with HIV, the mentally ill and children, as well as equity in healthcare. In the reproductive sphere: abortion, contraception, artificial insemination, in vitro fertilisation and surrogate motherhood. In genetics and cell technologies: genetic diagnostics, gene therapy, engineering, stem cells, therapeutic and reproductive cloning. At the end of life: care for the seriously ill, hospice and palliative care, suicide and euthanasia, passive or active.

t: The three faces of bioethics, its aim and task
n: The three faces of bioethics, its aim and task. First, bioethics is a multidisciplinary field that studies the consequences of progress in biomedicine: the physician, biologist, philosopher and lawyer work together. Second, it is a sphere of academic and educational activity; third, it is a rapidly developing social institution, that is, international, national and local committees. The aim: to seek an ethical and legal solution to non-traditional situations connected with the beginning and end of life and with intervention. The task: to develop a theory of the legal protection of the individual and to put it into practice.

Principles, rules and UNESCO documents. The principles of the biomedical model are five: autonomy, informed consent, non-maleficence, confidentiality and truthfulness. In the 2005 declaration the interests of the individual are placed above the interests of science and society. Among UNESCO documents, the Declaration on the Human Genome was adopted in 1997, the document on genetic data in 2003, and the Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights in 2005. Attention: principles are not a ready-made order to the physician, but a basis for reaching a specific decision.

Beauchamp and Childress advance four basic principles: respect for autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence and justice. The principles have no hierarchical order; they are considered equal. Autonomy means free choice, that is, consent or refusal. “Do no harm”, in Latin “Primum non nocere”, that is, “first, do no harm”, goes back to Hippocratic ethics. Beneficence means preserving life and relieving suffering. Justice: help is provided regardless of sex, age, race, nationality, social status and belief.

Let us summarise. Ethics was founded by Aristotle; applied ethics applies it to specific situations, and bioethics arose along this path in the second half of the twentieth century. Potter introduced the term “bioethics”, Schweitzer founded the ethics of “reverence for life”, and the Nuremberg Code, 1947, made the responsibility of scientists an international issue. There are four models of medical ethics: Hippocratic, Paracelsian, deontological and biomedical; the structure of bioethics also has four parts. The principles of the biomedical model are autonomy, informed consent, non-maleficence, confidentiality and truthfulness.
